docs.title: 🧠 Investigation workflow
docs.text:
1. Scope the data — logs, PCAPs, and timestamps
  2. Build a timeline — what happened first through last
  3. Validate hypotheses — Splunk searches and packet inspection
  4. Extract IOCs — IPs, domains, user agents where applicable
  5. Detection ideas — how this would be caught in a real SOC

docs.title: 🧰 Tools & skills
docs.text:
• SIEM / log analysis: Splunk (search, stats, pivots)
  • Network analysis: Wireshark (filters, protocol inspection)
  • Reporting: structured writeups with evidence and reasoning

docs.title: ✅ Responsible sharing
docs.text: These writeups avoid publishing flags or sensitive spoilers and focus on methodology, evidence, and detection thinking.

docs.title: Scenario context
docs.text:
An internal SOC alert flagged an unusual VPN login for a corporate user. While initial context suggested the user might be traveling, SOC procedures required validation of the source IP and any associated artifacts before determining whether the activity was benign.

This task focused on: - IP reputation and infrastructure analysis - Malware identification and classification - Threat intelligence enrichment using external reports

docs.title: IP attribution and service classification
docs.text:
Objective: Determine whether the source IP involved in the VPN login belonged to legitimate infrastructure or was associated with malicious activity.

Action: The IP address was reviewed using internal threat intelligence tooling to identify ownership and service characteristics.

Findings: - The IP was associated with ASN 212238 - The infrastructure was identified as offering VPN services

Assessment: Although VPN usage can be legitimate, adversaries frequently abuse rented or anonymized VPN infrastructure. This warranted further investigation rather than immediate dismissal as a false positive.

docs.title: File hash analysis
docs.text:
Objective: Determine the nature of a suspicious binary associated with the investigation.

Action: The provided SHA-256 hash was searched in the internal threat intelligence platform TryDetectThis to retrieve file metadata and detection results.

Evidence:

Findings: - Filename: zY9sqWs.exe - File type: Windows executable - The file was detected by multiple security vendors as malicious - YARA detection linked the binary to known malware families

Assessment: The presence of a malicious executable strongly indicated that the VPN login was not benign and required deeper threat intelligence enrichment.

docs.title: Threat signature and malware family
docs.text:
Objective: Identify how major security vendors classify the malware.

Action: Vendor intelligence was reviewed for threat naming and classification.

Findings: - Microsoft classified the malware as: Trojan:Win32/LummaStealer.PM!MTB

Assessment: LummaStealer is a known infostealer malware family associated with credential theft, data exfiltration, and affiliate-based distribution models.

docs.title: Infrastructure clustering
docs.text:
Objective: Determine whether the malware was part of a broader malicious infrastructure.

Action: TLS certificate metadata associated with one of the contacted domains was analyzed.

Findings: - 151 domains were linked to the same campaign based on HTTPS certificate reuse

Assessment: Large-scale infrastructure reuse is a strong indicator of organized malicious campaigns rather than isolated activity.

docs.title: YARA rule validation
docs.text:
Objective: Understand why the suspicious binary was flagged by rule-based detection and validate the logic used to identify it.

Action: The YARA rule authored by kevoreilly that matched the file was reviewed, focusing on the condition used to trigger detection.

docs.title: YARA rule analysis
docs.text:
Objective: Validate how the malware was detected at a rule-based level.

Action: The matched YARA rule authored by kevoreilly was reviewed.

Findings: - The following condition was present in the rule: uint16(0) == 0x5a4d and any of them

Assessment: This condition confirms the file is a valid Windows PE executable and matches one or more behavioral or structural indicators defined in the rule.

docs.title: External threat intelligence correlation
docs.text:
Objective: Identify whether the malware had been documented in public or private threat intelligence reports.

Action: Threat intelligence reports referencing the hash were reviewed.

Findings: - The hash was mentioned in the report titled: “Behind the Curtain: How Lumma Affiliates Operate”

Assessment: Presence in a dedicated threat intelligence report further confirms the malware’s relevance and operational use in active campaigns.

docs.title: Affiliate behavior and related tooling
docs.text:
Objective: Understand the broader affiliate ecosystem associated with the malware.

Findings: - The malware author began collaborating with the GhostSocks team in early 2024 - A Mexican-based affiliate associated with the malware also leveraged additional infostealers - One such infostealer targeting Android systems was identified as CraxsRAT

Assessment: Cross-platform targeting (Windows and Android) highlights the expanding scope and maturity of the affiliate ecosystem.

docs.title: ATT&CK technique alignment
docs.text:
Objective: Map observed adversary behavior to MITRE ATT&CK techniques to better understand infrastructure acquisition patterns.

Action: Threat intelligence findings related to anonymized infrastructure usage were mapped against the MITRE ATT&CK framework.

Evidence:

Findings: - The activity aligns with: T1583.003 – Acquire Infrastructure: Virtual Private Server

Assessment: Adversaries commonly leverage rented VPS infrastructure to host malicious services such as command-and-control servers, allowing rapid provisioning and reduced attribution risk. This mapping supports the hypothesis that the observed activity was part of an organized malicious campaign rather than incidental misuse.

docs.title: Task conclusion
docs.text:
Initial assumptions suggested the VPN login might be benign due to user travel. However, layered analysis revealed:

  • Use of suspicious VPN infrastructure
  • Presence of confirmed malware
  • Association with a large-scale malicious campaign
  • Documented use by organized affiliate networks

Based on these findings, the activity could not be classified as a false positive and required escalation for further investigation.
